title: Fine-Tuning LLMs
subtitle: When and how to fine-tune vs prompt engineer
author: KERNAL Team

whyItExists.problem: Even with excellent prompting, models may inconsistently follow a very specific style, produce a unique output format, or excel at a highly domain-specific task. When consistency is required at scale and prompting has reached its limits, fine-tuning is the next lever.
whyItExists.solution: Fine-tuning trains model weights on your curated input-output examples, ingraining specific behavior. The result is a model that consistently behaves as desired without large system prompts per request.
whyItExists.whenToUse: When prompt engineering is inconsistent at scale, when you need to reduce system prompt size (cost), when output style/format needs to be exact and reproducible, when you have 100+ high-quality labeled examples.
whyItExists.whenNotToUse: To inject new factual knowledge (use RAG instead), when you have <50 examples, when the task can be solved with better prompting, early in a project before you understand requirements.

explainModes.beginner: Imagine training a new employee for 3 months versus giving a smart contractor a detailed briefing each time. Fine-tuning is the 3-month training — after it, the model 'just knows' your style. Prompting is the contractor briefing — works great but you repeat it every time.
explainModes.simple: Fine-tuning updates the model's weights using your examples so it permanently learns your specific style or format. The fine-tuned model behaves differently from the base model without needing a large system prompt every request.
explainModes.standard: Fine-tuning creates a new model checkpoint by continuing training on a small labeled dataset of (input, output) pairs. It's supervised learning on your data — gradient descent updates the weights to better reproduce your outputs. The result is cheaper per request (smaller prompts) and more consistent formatting.
explainModes.technical: OpenAI fine-tuning: upload a JSONL file of {messages: [{role, content}]} objects, create a fine-tuning job, wait for training, then use the fine_tuned_model ID. Full fine-tuning updates all weights. LoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation) only trains small rank-decomposition matrices, reducing trainable parameters by ~1000x — much cheaper and prevents catastrophic forgetting.
explainModes.deepDive: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) methods: LoRA (adds low-rank matrices A, B to attention layers, trains only A and B), QLoRA (quantised LoRA on 4-bit base models), prefix tuning (learnable prefix tokens), adapter modules. RLHF (Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback) uses a reward model trained on human preferences to fine-tune with PPO — the technique behind ChatGPT's alignment. DPO (Direct Preference Optimisation) achieves similar results without the RL loop.

content.text: Fine-tuning trains the model's weights on your data, permanently specialising its behaviour. It is expensive and usually unnecessary — good prompting covers 90% of use cases. But when consistency and style precision are critical at scale, fine-tuning unlocks the remaining 10%.

a.name: Prompt Engineering
a.description: No training — instructions and examples in every request
weaknesses: Large system prompts cost tokens every request
a.useWhen: Starting any project. 90% of tasks. When style consistency isn't mission-critical.

b.name: Fine-Tuning
b.description: New model checkpoint trained on your labeled examples
strengths: Smaller prompts per request (cost savings at scale)
Can learn task-specific patterns beyond prompting's reach
b.useWhen: High-volume production (millions of requests), very specific style requirements, reducing per-request costs when system prompt is large.

content.code:
from openai import OpenAI
import json

client = OpenAI()

# Step 1: Prepare training data (JSONL format)
training_examples = [
    {
        "messages": [
            {"role": "system", "content": "You write product descriptions in our brand voice: confident, friendly, and focused on benefits."},
            {"role": "user", "content": "Product: Wireless noise-cancelling headphones with 30h battery"},
            {"role": "assistant", "content": "Drown out the world. These headphones wrap you in silence so you can focus, create, or just breathe — for up to 30 hours without reaching for a charger."}
        ]
    },
    # ... 100+ more examples
]

# Write to JSONL file
with open("training_data.jsonl", "w") as f:
    for ex in training_examples:
        f.write(json.dumps(ex) + "\n")

# Step 2: Upload training file
upload = client.files.create(
    file=open("training_data.jsonl", "rb"),
    purpose="fine-tune"
)
print(f"File ID: {upload.id}")

# Step 3: Create fine-tuning job
job = client.fine_tuning.jobs.create(
    training_file=upload.id,
    model="gpt-4o-mini",  # cheap base model
    hyperparameters={"n_epochs": 3}
)
print(f"Job ID: {job.id}")

# Step 4: Check status (poll or use webhooks)
status = client.fine_tuning.jobs.retrieve(job.id)
print(f"Status: {status.status}")  # validating_files → running → succeeded

from openai import OpenAI
client = OpenAI()

# Step 5: Use your fine-tuned model (no system prompt needed!)
FINE_TUNED_MODEL = "ft:gpt-4o-mini:your-org:product-copy:AbCd1234"

response = client.chat.completions.create(
    model=FINE_TUNED_MODEL,
    messages=[{
        "role": "user",
        "content": "Product: Reusable bamboo coffee cups (4-pack)"
    }]
)
print(response.choices[0].message.content)
# Output is now consistently in your brand voice — no system prompt needed

content.text: LoRA: Efficient Fine-Tuning of Open Models

LoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation) fine-tunes open-source models (Llama, Mistral) by adding small trainable rank-decomposition matrices to attention layers. It trains 1000x fewer parameters than full fine-tuning — achievable on a single GPU in hours.

content.code:
# pip install peft transformers datasets
from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM, AutoTokenizer, TrainingArguments
from peft import LoraConfig, get_peft_model, TaskType
from trl import SFTTrainer

# Load base model (Llama or Mistral)
model_name = "mistralai/Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3"
model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(model_name, load_in_4bit=True)  # QLoRA
tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(model_name)

# Configure LoRA — only train rank-decomposition matrices
lora_config = LoraConfig(
    task_type=TaskType.CAUSAL_LM,
    r=16,            # rank of low-rank matrices
    lora_alpha=32,   # scaling factor
    lora_dropout=0.1,
    target_modules=["q_proj", "v_proj"]  # which attention layers
)
model = get_peft_model(model, lora_config)
model.print_trainable_parameters()  # e.g., 0.1% of total parameters!

# Train with SFTTrainer
trainer = SFTTrainer(
    model=model,
    train_dataset=your_dataset,  # Hugging Face dataset
    args=TrainingArguments(
        output_dir="./lora_output",
        per_device_train_batch_size=4,
        num_train_epochs=3,
    )
)
trainer.train()

content.text: Always try prompt engineering + few-shot examples before fine-tuning. Fine-tuning costs money, time, and locks you into static behavior. If prompting works at 95% quality, it's usually not worth fine-tuning for the remaining 5%.
Fine-tuning does NOT reliably add new factual knowledge. Use RAG for that. Fine-tuning is for style, format, and task specialisation. A fine-tuned model still hallucinates facts it doesn't know.

questions.question: When is fine-tuning most justified?
options: When you want to add new factual knowledge to the model
When you need consistent style/format at scale and prompting has reached its limits
Whenever you have more than 20 training examples
When you want faster response times
questions.explanation: Fine-tuning is best for ingraining specific style and format when prompting is inconsistent at high volumes. For new knowledge, use RAG. Fine-tuning doesn't reliably add facts.

questions.question: What is LoRA?
options: A vector database optimised for LLM embeddings
Low-Rank Adaptation — adds small trainable matrices to attention layers, reducing trainable params by ~1000x
A loss function for RLHF training
questions.explanation: LoRA adds low-rank rank-decomposition matrices (A and B) to existing weight matrices. Only A and B are trained — the base model stays frozen. This reduces trainable parameters to ~0.1% of full fine-tuning.

questions.question: What is the minimum recommended number of training examples for fine-tuning?
options: Fine-tuning works with any amount of data
questions.explanation: 50-100 high-quality examples are typically the minimum. Quality matters more than quantity — 50 perfect examples outperform 1000 noisy ones. For complex tasks, 500-1000 examples.

faq.a: Anthropic offers fine-tuning for select enterprise customers through their API. For most developers, prompt engineering with the base model is the recommended path. OpenAI offers fine-tuning on gpt-4o-mini and gpt-3.5-turbo for all API customers.
When fine-tuning on a narrow dataset, models can 'forget' general capabilities. LoRA mitigates this because the base model weights stay frozen — only the small adapters are trained.

OpenAI gpt-4o-mini fine-tuning: ~$3/1M training tokens. A typical dataset of 1000 examples × 500 tokens = 500K tokens → ~$1.50 to train. Inference with the fine-tuned model costs ~2x the base model. Hugging Face LoRA on Mistral-7B: free on a rented A100 GPU for a few hours.

usedIn: Brand-voice content generation at scale (marketing teams)
Legal/medical document summarisation with domain-specific output format
Customer service response generation with consistent tone
Code style enforcement (always generate in company's coding conventions)
examples: A marketing SaaS fine-tunes gpt-4o-mini on 500 approved product descriptions to consistently output in brand voice — eliminating the 400-token system prompt per request
A legal firm fine-tunes Llama 3 with LoRA on 1000 contract summaries to match their specific clause structure
